**TREASURY HILL BRIEF** | Morning Edition | Public-Source Prototype

---

**TOP LINE**
H.R. 7148, the FY2026 consolidated appropriations act, is now law (P.L. 119-75), setting discretionary funding for Treasury, IRS, and FinCEN. Ways and Means advanced six IRS-related bills on strong bipartisan votes. The FinCEN oversight hearing is the primary floor-level Treasury exposure today.

---

**NOMINATIONS**
Nine Treasury nominations remain stalled in the Finance Committee pipeline. Deputy Secretary Brooke (55d referred) and Chief Counsel Gadwood (12d) are highest priority. Two nominees were withdrawn; one was returned. No floor votes scheduled.

---

**LEGISLATION AND RULES**
Ways and Means ordered to report six bills: IRS workforce modernization (H.R. 7972, 24-16), tax-exempt hospital transparency (H.R. 9504, 25-15), hostage tax relief (H.R. 9496, 40-0), Taxpayer Advocate expansion (H.R. 9498, 39-0), fraud victim relief (H.R. 9500, 39-0), AI tax integrity (H.R. 9501, 40-0), and ghost preparer penalties (H.R. 9499, 40-0). Recent Treasury rules updated Venezuela, Iran, and North Korea sanctions general licenses.

---

**HEARINGS**
House Financial Services Subcommittee holds FinCEN oversight hearing. Witness: Director Andrea Gacki.

**TREASURY HILL BRIEF**
*Prototype — Public Sources Only — Not an Official Product*

---

**TOP LINE**
FY2026 omnibus (H.R. 7148) is now law, setting Treasury and IRS discretionary funding for the full fiscal year. Ways and Means advanced six IRS-related bills unanimously, signaling fast floor movement. FinCEN Director Gacki faces subcommittee oversight this week.

---

**NOMINATIONS**
Nine Treasury nominees remain stalled. Francis Brooke (Deputy Secretary) has sat in committee 54 days. Erin Browne (Under Secretary) at 82 days. Kothari (Asst. Secretary) was returned after 172 days and re-referred. Korb, Trennert, and Petit nominations were withdrawn after delays of 228, 339, and 508 days respectively.

---

**LEGISLATION AND RULES**
Ways and Means ordered six bills reported, all with strong bipartisan votes: Taxpayer Workforce Modernization Act, Tax Exempt Hospital Transparency Act, Tax Relief for Fraud Victims Act, Taxpayer Advocate Participation Act, End Tax Penalties on American Hostages Act, AI Tax Integrity Act, and Ghost Preparers Act. Treasury published updated Venezuela, Iran, and North Korea sanctions guidance in June. Financial Data Transparency Act joint data standards also published.

---

**HEARINGS**
House Financial Services Subcommittee is conducting oversight of FinCEN. Director Andrea Gacki is the sole witness.

**TREASURY LEGISLATIVE AFFAIRS — MORNING HILL BRIEF**
*Public-source prototype. Not an official product.*

---

**TOP LINE**
FY2026 appropriations are enacted (P.L. 119-75), setting binding funding ceilings for IRS, FinCEN, OFR, and Departmental Offices. Recent OFAC activity includes updated Venezuela and Iran general licenses and a revised North Korea medical device authorization list. Financial Data Transparency Act joint data standards published June 25.

---

**NOMINATIONS**
Nine Treasury nominations are stalled. Francis Brooke (Deputy Secretary) has been in referral 53 days. Erin Browne (Under Secretary) sits at 81 days. Kothari (Assistant Secretary) was returned after 181 days. Three nominations have been withdrawn: Korb, Trennert, and Petit. Gadwood (IRS Chief Counsel) was referred 10 days ago.

---

**LEGISLATION & RULES**
Active Ways and Means referrals include rental housing tax incentives (H.R. 9573), a windfall profits excise tax on major oil companies (H.R. 7960), and retirement savings eligibility expansion (H.R. 4718). Treasury published escrow account lending standards June 29.

---

**HEARINGS**
House Financial Services Subcommittee is conducting oversight of FinCEN. Director Andrea Gacki is the witness.

**TREASURY HILL BRIEF** | Morning Edition | Public-Source Prototype

---

**TOP LINE**
Four Treasury nominees remain stalled in committee, the longest at 170 days. Two prior nominees were withdrawn without confirmation. Semiconductor tax credit bills advanced in both chambers. OFAC published Iran, Venezuela, and North Korea sanctions updates in June.

---

**NOMINATIONS**
Francis Brooke (Deputy Secretary) stalled 52 days. George McMaster (Asst. Secretary) 66 days. Erin Browne (Under Secretary) 80 days. Kothari (Asst. Secretary) referred 170 days; a prior Kothari nomination was returned. Gadwood (IRS Chief Counsel) referred 9 days. Three prior nominees withdrawn without confirmation.

---

**LEGISLATION & RULES**
Semiconductor Superiority Act advanced in both chambers (H.R. 8959, S. 4750); Treasury/IRS face Section 48D credit implementation obligations. H.R. 9267 and S. 4657 referred to tax-jurisdiction committees; Office of Tax Policy should assess revenue exposure. H.R. 6556 (Failing Bank Acquisition Fairness Act) placed on Union Calendar; implications for orderly liquidation authority. Recent OFAC actions updated Iran, Venezuela, and North Korea general licenses.

---

**HEARINGS**
House Financial Services Subcommittee: Oversight of FinCEN. Witness: Director Andrea Gacki.

# House Financial Services Committee Hearing Prep
## Witness Topic: Corporate Transparency Act / BOI, AML Modernization, Crypto Illicit Finance
### Democratic Members — Minority Bench

---

## Maxine Waters (D-CA) — Ranking Member

**Line 1: CTA Implementation and Rollback Concerns**
Waters has been a consistent critic of any administration action she perceives as weakening financial crime enforcement. She is likely to press on whether Treasury's FinCEN has scaled back BOI reporting requirements under current regulatory guidance, and whether any exemptions benefit politically connected entities or large corporations at the expense of smaller illicit actors who remain unchecked.

**Line 2: Racial Equity in AML Enforcement**
Waters frequently ties financial regulation to fair enforcement outcomes. She is likely to raise whether AML examination practices disproportionately burden minority-owned community banks and credit unions while larger institutions receive deferred prosecution agreements or modest penalties relative to their violations.

**Suggested Response Posture:**
Acknowledge the oversight role of the committee directly and respectfully. Affirm commitment to robust BOI data collection while citing specific FinCEN rulemakings and enforcement statistics. On equity concerns, offer to provide the committee with disaggregated examination data where available and commit to a follow-up briefing rather than debating specific cases on the record.

---

## Nydia M. Velázquez (D-NY)

**Line 1: Small Business Compliance Burden Under CTA**
Velázquez chairs or has long served on the Small Business Committee and is deeply attentive to regulatory compliance costs on small enterprises. She is likely to ask whether Treasury has conducted sufficient outreach to small business owners, particularly immigrant-owned businesses and minority entrepreneurs, about BOI filing obligations, and whether the penalty structure is proportionate for good-faith non-filers.

**Line 2: Remittance Corridor AML Friction**
Velázquez represents a large Puerto Rican and Dominican-American constituency. She is likely to raise how AML de-risking by banks has reduced access to affordable remittance services for her constituents, and whether FinCEN guidance has done enough to distinguish legitimate remittance flows from illicit ones.

**Suggested Response Posture:**
Lead with concrete figures on FinCEN's small business education campaign, including outreach events, multilingual materials, and the penalty mitigation provisions for good-faith violations. On remittances, cite the joint agency guidance on de-risking and acknowledge the tension between AML compliance incentives and financial access. Avoid appearing dismissive of constituent-level impact.

---

## Brad Sherman (D-CA)

**Line 1: Crypto as a Sanctions and AML Evasion Vector**
Sherman has been among the most aggressive critics of cryptocurrency in the committee, frequently citing its use in sanctions evasion by Iran, North Korea, and Russia. He is likely to ask whether Treasury believes current crypto AML rules are adequate, whether DeFi platforms present a gap in the regulatory perimeter, and whether OFAC has the technical capacity to enforce sanctions against decentralized protocols.

**Line 2: Adequacy of Crypto Exchange Compliance**
Sherman is likely to question whether major centralized crypto exchanges are genuinely implementing Bank Secrecy Act obligations or whether FinCEN's examination of these entities is sufficiently rigorous. He may cite specific enforcement cases or GAO findings to suggest the regime is under-enforced.

**Suggested Response Posture:**
Do not be defensive about crypto enforcement gaps. Acknowledge that the regulatory framework for DeFi and decentralized protocols presents novel jurisdictional challenges and that Treasury is actively engaged with interagency partners and Congress on legislative solutions. Cite concrete enforcement actions, including OFAC designations and FinCEN penalties against crypto platforms, without overstating their deterrent effect.

---

## Gregory W. Meeks (D-NY)

**Line 1: AML Compliance and Correspondent Banking in the Caribbean**
Meeks, as former chair of the Foreign Affairs Committee, is attentive to how U.S. AML policy affects Caribbean nations. He is likely to raise whether de-risking by U.S. correspondent banks is strangling legitimate financial flows to Caribbean economies and whether Treasury has a coherent strategy to address this without relaxing AML standards.

**Line 2: Illicit Finance Through Trade-Based Money Laundering**
Meeks may raise trade-based money laundering as an underenforced vector, particularly as it relates to import and export flows through New York and to developing economies in his areas of foreign policy focus. He is likely to ask what Treasury is doing to modernize trade finance AML oversight.

**Suggested Response Posture:**
Affirm that correspondent banking de-risking is a recognized problem and reference the Treasury-led efforts in the Financial Stability Board and FATF to develop proportionate AML standards for correspondent relationships. On trade-based money laundering, acknowledge it is one of the least-examined vectors and point to any interagency working group activity or pilot programs while being honest about resource constraints.

---

## Stephen F. Lynch (D-MA)

**Line 1: FinCEN BOI Database Access Controls and Law Enforcement Utility**
Lynch has been closely involved in AML legislation and is likely to probe whether the BOI database is actually being used effectively by law enforcement. He may ask how many law enforcement queries have been made, what the access protocols are, and whether financial institutions have been granted the access they need to make BOI data useful for their own compliance programs.

**Line 2: Correspondent Bank Monitoring and Shell Company Abuse**
Lynch has focused on shell company abuse in prior hearings. He is likely to ask whether the CTA's beneficial ownership definitions contain loopholes that sophisticated actors can exploit, particularly through layered ownership structures involving trusts or nominee arrangements.

**Suggested Response Posture:**
Come prepared with specific data on BOI database query volume and user categories if available or indicate clearly that you will provide it in writing. On definitional gaps, acknowledge that the implementing regulations made deliberate tradeoffs to maintain administrability and that Treasury is monitoring whether those tradeoffs are being exploited. Avoid implying the rule is final and immutable.

---

## Al Green (D-TX)

**Line 1: Enforcement Disparities in AML Penalties**
Green has a consistent focus on whether large financial institutions receive accountability commensurate with their violations. He is likely to argue that major bank AML failures result in deferred prosecution agreements while smaller or minority-serving institutions face charter threats, and ask what Treasury is doing to ensure proportional and racially equitable enforcement.

bills.title: To amend the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to provide incentives for certain residential rental property.
bills.status: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
bills.nexus: H.R. 9573 directly implicates IRS and Treasury's Office of Tax Policy, as any amendment to the Internal Revenue Code requires Treasury to develop implementing regulations and guidance. Treasury must assess revenue cost, potential compliance risks, and administrative burden on IRS before the bill advances beyond Ways and Means.

bills.title: Taxpayer Workforce Modernization Act
bills.status: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 24 - 16.
bills.nexus: H.R. 7972 directly implicates IRS workforce authorities under Treasury's oversight, touching hiring flexibilities, compensation structures, and potentially civil service classifications for IRS personnel. The implementation risk centers on Treasury and IRS absorbing new statutory mandates for workforce restructuring while managing ongoing modernization initiatives under the Inflation Reduction Act funding baseline.

bills.title: Tax Exempt Hospital Transparency Act
bills.status: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 25 - 15.
bills.nexus: H.R. 9504 directly implicates the IRS (a Treasury bureau) because it would modify the tax-exempt status requirements and Schedule H reporting obligations governing nonprofit hospitals under Section 501(r) of the Internal Revenue Code. Treasury's implementation risk centers on IRS capacity to process expanded disclosure data and potentially revoke exemptions, raising both administrative burden and revenue baseline concerns.

bills.title: End Tax Penalties on American Hostages Act
bills.status: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 40 - 0.
bills.nexus: H.R. 9496 directly implicates IRS authority under the Internal Revenue Code by requiring the Service to waive tax penalties and interest for Americans wrongfully detained or held hostage abroad during the period of their captivity. Treasury and IRS must assess the administrative mechanics of identifying qualifying individuals, processing penalty abatements, and accounting for any resulting revenue loss, while ensuring the relief framework does not create compliance or fraud vulnerabilities.

bills.title: Taxpayer Advocate Participation Act
bills.status: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 39 - 0.
bills.nexus: H.R. 9498 directly affects the Office of the Taxpayer Advocate (OTA) under IRC Section 7803(c) by expanding taxpayer rights to request Advocate participation during IRS examinations or collection proceedings. Treasury's implementation risk centers on potential resource strain on OTA and the need for regulatory guidance defining the scope and limits of mandated participation.

bills.title: Tax Relief for Fraud Victims Act
bills.status: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 39 - 0.
bills.nexus: H.R. 9500 directly engages IRS authority under the Internal Revenue Code by modifying tax treatment for victims of fraud-related losses, falling within the Office of Tax Policy's purview on casualty and theft loss deduction rules. The unanimous committee vote signals likely floor consideration, requiring IRS to develop administrative guidance and potentially update Form 4684 instructions, creating near-term implementation burden and revenue-scoring obligations for the Joint Committee on Taxation.

bills.title: AI Tax Integrity Act of 2026
bills.status: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 40 - 0.
bills.nexus:
Without a known nexus provided, here is a placeholder briefing based on the bill title alone:

H.R. 9501 would direct IRS (under Treasury's authority over tax administration and enforcement) to develop standards or rules governing AI use in tax compliance and examination processes. Treasury's Office of Tax Policy and IRS would bear primary implementation responsibility, and the bill creates operational and legal risk around how AI-assisted determinations affect taxpayer rights and audit defensibility.

bills.title: Protecting Taxpayers from Ghost Preparers Act
bills.status: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 40 - 0.
bills.nexus: H.R. 9499 directly implicates IRS authority under the Internal Revenue Code to regulate and sanction paid tax return preparers, touching the IRS Return Preparer Office and its enforcement jurisdiction. The implementation risk centers on whether IRS has sufficient statutory authority and resources to identify, penalize, and enjoin "ghost preparers" who prepare returns for compensation without signing them, creating both taxpayer harm and tax gap exposure.

bills.title: Credit Access and Inclusion Act of 2025
bills.status: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 28 - 23.
bills.nexus: H.R. 5402 would amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act to allow reporting of on-time utility, telecom, and rental payment data to consumer reporting agencies, directly implicating Treasury's Office of Consumer Policy and its work on financial inclusion and credit market access. The narrow committee margin (28-23) signals contested implementation questions around data accuracy, consumer harm safeguards, and potential downstream effects on federally supervised lenders and credit markets that Treasury monitors.

bills.title: Community Flood Resilience Act
bills.status: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
bills.nexus: H.R. 9056 directly implicates the Federal Insurance Office (FIO) and Treasury's oversight role under the National Flood Insurance Program's fiscal exposure, which sits on the federal balance sheet. Treasury cares because expanded flood resilience mandates or coverage changes could alter federal reinsurance arrangements, shift actuarial risk, and create budget scoring implications requiring interagency coordination with FEMA and OMB.

bills.title: Expressing support for the work of open water lifeguards as first responders and emergency response providers.
bills.status: Referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
bills.nexus: H.Res. 1188 is a simple House resolution honoring open water lifeguards and does not touch any Treasury office, tax provision, financial regulatory authority, or appropriations stream. Treasury has no implementation role, fiscal exposure, or policy equities in this measure.

bills.title: Big Oil Windfall Profits Tax Act
bills.status: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
bills.nexus: H.R. 7960 directly implicates the Internal Revenue Service and the Office of Tax Policy, as it would impose an excise tax on major integrated oil companies' quarterly profits exceeding a pre-pandemic baseline. Treasury bears implementation risk through the need to promulgate regulations defining "windfall profit," establish quarterly reporting mechanisms, and administer refundable consumer rebate credits tied to the new revenue stream.

bills.title: Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026
bills.nexus: H.R. 7148 directly governs discretionary funding levels for the Department of the Treasury, including appropriations for IRS operations, the Office of Financial Research, and Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN). Treasury's implementation risk centers on budget execution across these bureaus, potential continuing-resolution carryover constraints, and maintaining compliance with any new legislative riders or reporting mandates embedded in the act.

bills.title: Helping Young Americans Save for Retirement Act
bills.status: Referred to the Committee on Ways and Means, and in addition to the Committee on Education and Workforce, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.
bills.nexus: H.R. 4718 directly implicates Treasury's Office of Tax Policy and IRS, as it would amend Internal Revenue Code provisions governing tax-advantaged retirement accounts to allow younger workers, likely those under current age thresholds, to participate in or contribute to qualified plans. Treasury faces implementation risk in issuing conforming regulations and updating IRS plan qualification guidance to reflect any new eligibility rules without disrupting existing plan administration.
